READ-ONLY security audit of Nxeon auth/session/RBAC and IDOR in /opt/nxeon (Next.js 15 App Router, server actions in lib/actions-*.ts + route handlers in app/api/**). Do NOT edit/build/mutate — investigation only. Report findings with exact file:line, exploit sketch, and fix.

Start by reading lib/auth.ts, lib/rbac.ts, lib/api-auth.ts, lib/team-guard.ts, lib/admin-groups.ts to understand the session model, how getSession/requireUser/requireAdmin work, and how ownership is enforced.

Then hunt for:
1. Account takeover — password reset (app/reset-password, app/forgot-password, lib/actions-account.ts, lib/email-verification.ts): is the reset token high-entropy, single-use, time-limited, and bound to the user? Any user-enumeration or token-in-URL leak? 2FA/TOTP bypass — lib/totp.ts, lib/totp-verify.ts, lib/actions-2fa.ts. Session fixation, cookie flags (httpOnly/secure/sameSite) in lib/auth.ts. JWT/jose secret handling.
2. Privilege escalation — can a normal user reach admin server actions or /app/admin/** or /app/api/admin/**? Is requireAdmin/RBAC checked at the START of every admin action, not just in the UI? Look at lib/actions-staff.ts, lib/actions-admin-billing.ts, lib/actions-improvements.ts, lib/actions-board.ts, lib/actions-nodes.ts. Can a user set their own role/isAdmin via a profile/settings update (mass-assignment)? Check lib/actions-account.ts, lib/actions-settings.ts, lib/actions-prefs.ts, lib/actions-teams.ts for updates that spread untrusted input into prisma update data.
3. IDOR — this is the priority. Enumerate route handlers under app/api/** that take an [id] param and server actions that take an id/resourceId argument, and for EACH check whether it verifies the resource belongs to the caller (WHERE userId = session.user.id, or team membership) BEFORE reading/mutating. High-value targets: servers, invoices (app/api/invoices, lib/invoices.ts, lib/invoice-pdf.ts), domains, hosting accounts, databases, files, support tickets, teams, backups, mailboxes, coldemail, board cards, chat. Find any action that does prisma.X.findUnique({where:{id}}) / update({where:{id}}) using ONLY the id from the request without an ownership predicate. Report each as an IDOR with the file:line and what an attacker reads/mutates.

Give me a ranked list CRITICAL/HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW with file:line. Prioritize CONCRETE IDOR/priv-esc with a clear ownership-check gap over theoretical issues. Honest verdict on the overall auth posture. Return findings as final message text, not a file.

2	 * Team invitations: consent tokens, plus who is entitled to see whom.
3	 *
4	 * WHY THIS MODULE NO LONGER EXPORTS `requireArea`
5	 * ----------------------------------------------
6	 * It used to export `requireArea(orgId, area)` — a page guard for "org-scoped
7	 * dashboard pages". There were none: `requireArea` had zero call sites in the
8	 * repo (AUDIT-24H rec. 47, QA-PRELAUNCH P1-19), `memberCanAccessHref` was
9	 * referenced only from its own docblock, and `Membership.areas` was write-only.
10	 * Meanwhile the Team UI rendered a checkbox per dashboard area and reported
11	 * "Access updated." So an owner who unticked everything except Invoices was
12	 * shown a restriction that no loader, action or route ever consulted. That is
13	 * the same defect class as the fake SSL certs and the migration that logged 4/4
14	 * with six domains dark, and it is the more dangerous shape of it: a security
15	 * control that reports success while enforcing nothing.
16	 *
17	 * Wiring it up for real would mean org-scoping every dashboard loader and every
18	 * server action that touches a server, domain, volume, invoice or ticket — none
19	 * of which live in this module's blast radius. A half-wired version (nav hidden,
20	 * loaders open) is strictly worse than none, because hiding a nav item looks
21	 * like enforcement. So the area system is deleted rather than faked, and this
22	 * module now carries the two things teams genuinely need in order to be safe.
23	 *
24	 * 1. INVITE TOKENS (consent). `inviteMember` used to create a Membership
25	 *    outright — the invitee never agreed to anything — and the team page then
26	 *    handed the inviter every co-member's `userId` and email. That is precisely
27	 *    the identity feed that made the unauthenticated 2FA oracle
28	 *    (`verifyTotpForUser`, QA-PRELAUNCH P0-2) targetable at a named account:
29	 *    type a victim's email, get back their internal id. Membership now requires
30	 *    the invitee to click Accept while signed in as the invited address.
31	 *
32	 * 2. `canAdministerOrg` — the single definition of "may administer membership",
33	 *    used both to authorise mutations and to decide whether a viewer is
34	 *    entitled to co-members' email addresses.
35	 *
36	 * Plain server-side module (no "use server"), so both the server actions and the
37	 * accept page can import these helpers. Nothing here is client-safe.
38	 */
39	import { createHash } from "node:crypto";
40	import { EncryptJWT, jwtDecrypt } from "jose";
41	
42	/**
43	 * Invitation lifetime. Short on purpose: the token is the entire invitation
44	 * (see below), so expiry is the only thing that eventually retires a link the
45	 * sender regrets.
46	 */
47	export const INVITE_TTL_HOURS = 72;
48	
49	/** What an invitation carries. `invitedBy` is re-checked at accept time. */
50	export type InviteClaims = {
51	  orgId: string;
52	  /** Lowercased email the invitation was addressed to. Binds the link to one person. */
53	  email: string;
54	  role: string;
55	  invitedBy: string;
56	};
57	
58	/**
59	 * 256-bit key for the invite JWE, derived from AUTH_SECRET with an
60	 * invite-specific salt — the same derivation pattern as lib/terminal-token.ts.
61	 * The distinct salt means a session cookie can never be replayed as an
62	 * invitation (or vice-versa) even though both trace back to one secret.
63	 */
64	function inviteKey(): Uint8Array {
65	  const secret = process.env.AUTH_SECRET;
66	  if (!secret) throw new Error("AUTH_SECRET is not set — cannot issue team invitations");
67	  return new Uint8Array(createHash("sha256").update(`nxeon-org-invite:${secret}`).digest());
68	}
69	
70	/**
71	 * Mint an invitation token.
72	 *
73	 * ENCRYPTED (JWE, A256GCM), not merely signed. A signed JWT's payload is
74	 * readable by anyone holding the link, and this payload contains the inviter's
75	 * `userId` — the exact value the 2FA oracle needed (P0-2). An invitation that
76	 * leaked an internal user id to whoever opened the email would reintroduce the
77	 * hole this change exists to close, so the token is opaque to its bearer.
78	 *
79	 * STATELESS by necessity: prisma/schema.prisma has no Invitation model and is
80	 * frozen for this change. The consequences are real and are stated plainly in
81	 * the UI rather than papered over — pending invitations cannot be listed, and
82	 * they cannot be revoked individually. What limits them instead:
83	 *   - they expire (INVITE_TTL_HOURS);
84	 *   - `acceptInvite` re-verifies that the inviter STILL holds OWNER/ADMIN in the
85	 *     org, so demoting or removing an admin voids their outstanding invitations;
86	 *   - they are bound to one email address, so a forwarded link is useless.
87	 * If pending-invite listing/revocation is wanted, that needs a schema field —
88	 * an `Invitation` model (orgId, email, role, invitedById, tokenHash, expiresAt,
89	 * acceptedAt, revokedAt) is the missing piece.
90	 */
91	export async function signInviteToken(claims: InviteClaims): Promise<string> {
92	  return new EncryptJWT({
93	    // `kind` is belt-and-braces on top of the salted key: any token that decrypts
94	    // but wasn't minted here is rejected rather than interpreted.
95	    kind: "org-invite",
96	    orgId: claims.orgId,
97	    email: claims.email,
98	    role: claims.role,
99	    invitedBy: claims.invitedBy,
100	  })
101	    .setProtectedHeader({ alg: "dir", enc: "A256GCM" })
102	    .setIssuedAt()
103	    .setExpirationTime(`${INVITE_TTL_HOURS}h`)
104	    .encrypt(inviteKey());
105	}

107	/**
108	 * Decrypt + validate an invitation token. Returns null for anything that isn't a
109	 * well-formed, unexpired invitation — tampered, truncated, expired, minted with
110	 * a different secret, or a token of some other kind. Never throws, so callers
111	 * can render one honest "invalid or expired" message without leaking which of
112	 * those it was.
113	 */
114	export async function verifyInviteToken(token: string): Promise<InviteClaims | null> {
115	  if (!token) return null;
116	  try {
117	    const { payload } = await jwtDecrypt(token, inviteKey());
118	    if (payload.kind !== "org-invite") return null;
119	    const { orgId, email, role, invitedBy } = payload as Record<string, unknown>;
120	    if (
121	      typeof orgId !== "string" ||
122	      typeof email !== "string" ||
123	      typeof role !== "string" ||
124	      typeof invitedBy !== "string" ||
125	      !orgId ||
126	      !email ||
127	      !role ||
128	      !invitedBy
129	    ) {
130	      return null;
131	    }
132	    return { orgId, email: email.toLowerCase(), role, invitedBy };
133	  } catch {
134	    return null;
135	  }
136	}

139	 * Roles that may administer membership (invite / change roles / remove) — and,
140	 * because the two questions have the same answer, the only viewers entitled to
141	 * see co-members' email addresses. A rank-and-file member gets the roster's
142	 * names; harvesting a list of addresses out of an org you were added to is how
143	 * the identity leak above was monetised.
144	 */
145	export function canAdministerOrg(role: string): boolean {
146	  return role === "OWNER" || role === "ADMIN";
147	}

1	/**
2	 * Email verification: proof that the address on an account belongs to the person
3	 * using it.
4	 *
5	 * WHY THIS EXISTS (QA-JOURNEY B4)
6	 * ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
7	 * Until now there was none. `register()` created the user, opened a session and
8	 * redirected to the dashboard, and the account could transact immediately.
9	 * Anyone could sign up with anyone else's address. For a hosting business that
10	 * is not a missing nicety, it is a missing foundation: root passwords, invoices,
11	 * expiry warnings and dunning notices all go to that address, and it is also the
12	 * only route back into a locked-out account. A typo sends a stranger someone's
13	 * server credentials; a throwaway address farms signup credit and referral
14	 * rewards at zero cost.
15	 *
16	 * WHAT VERIFICATION GATES — AND WHAT IT DELIBERATELY DOES NOT
17	 * ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
18	 * It does NOT block signing up, signing in, or using the portal. A gate on the
19	 * front door would be theatre: it would stop nobody who actually controls the
20	 * address, and it would strand a real customer at a blank screen the moment mail
21	 * was slow. Browsing an account that owns nothing costs us nothing.
22	 *
23	 * It DOES block buying and provisioning. The line is drawn there because an
24	 * unverified address means WE CANNOT REACH THE PERSON WE ARE ABOUT TO CHARGE —
25	 * not with the receipt, not with the renewal warning, not with the dunning
26	 * sequence that precedes a suspension, and not with the root password of the
27	 * machine we just built. Taking money under those conditions is the defect.
28	 *
29	 * It also does not block anything that RETURNS money or value: refunds,
30	 * downgrades, cancellations, backups and restores of an already-paid service.
31	 * Those either hand the customer something back or operate on a service that
32	 * already cleared this gate when it was bought. Blocking them would invent a new
33	 * dead end while preventing no harm — which is the failure this codebase keeps
34	 * having to remove.
35	 *
36	 * TWO DELIBERATE FAIL-OPEN ESCAPES
37	 * ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
38	 * A gate nobody can pass is worse than no gate, so this one refuses to become
39	 * one:
40	 *
41	 *  1. GRANDFATHERING. Accounts that predate the feature have `emailVerifiedAt`
42	 *     NULL because they were never asked, not because they failed. Enforcing
43	 *     against them would retroactively lock existing paying customers out of
44	 *     renewing servers they already own. They are exempted by CREATION DATE.
45	 *     Note what is NOT done: their `emailVerifiedAt` is not backfilled with a
46	 *     timestamp. That column is evidence, and writing "verified at 09:14" for an
47	 *     address nobody ever confirmed would be a fabricated audit fact — exactly
48	 *     the class of comfortable lie this codebase keeps finding in its own data.
49	 *
50	 *  2. MAIL NOT CONFIGURED. If the instance cannot send email at all, nobody can
51	 *     verify, so the gate would silently close the entire purchase funnel on a
52	 *     mail misconfiguration. It stands down instead, and says so in the log.
53	 *     `lib/prefs.ts` makes the same call for the same reason: when the mechanism
54	 *     that delivers the message is broken, guess towards the customer.
55	 */
56	
57	import { createHash, randomBytes } from "node:crypto";
58	import type { User } from "@prisma/client";
59	import { db } from "./db";
60	import { normalizeEmail } from "./email-normalize";
61	import { checkRateLimit } from "./rate-limit";
62	
63	/**
64	 * Accounts created strictly BEFORE this instant are exempt (see fail-open 1).
65	 *
66	 * Set to the moment verification shipped. It is a constant rather than a
67	 * setting because it is a historical fact about this database, not a policy
68	 * anyone should be able to retune — moving it forward would silently un-gate
69	 * every account signed up since, and moving it back would lock out customers who
70	 * did nothing wrong.
71	 */
72	export const VERIFICATION_ENFORCED_FROM = new Date("2026-07-27T00:00:00.000Z");
73	
74	/** How long a verification link stays usable. Matches the copy in the email. */
75	export const VERIFICATION_TTL_MS = 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000;
76	
77	/** Shape of a user this module can reason about (keeps callers cheap to test). */
78	export type VerifiableUser = Pick<User, "id" | "email" | "name" | "emailVerifiedAt" | "createdAt">;
79	
80	/** Has this account actually proved control of its address? */
81	export function isEmailVerified(user: Pick<VerifiableUser, "emailVerifiedAt">): boolean {
82	  return user.emailVerifiedAt != null;
83	}
84	
85	/** Does this account predate verification and therefore sit outside the gate? */
86	export function isGrandfathered(user: Pick<VerifiableUser, "createdAt">): boolean {
87	  return user.createdAt < VERIFICATION_ENFORCED_FROM;
88	}
89	
90	/**
91	 * Pure half of the gate: given a user and whether this instance can send mail,
92	 * may they spend/provision? Separated from the DB so the whole policy — the
93	 * grandfather clause, the mail escape, the ordering between them — is unit
94	 * testable without a database or an SMTP server.
95	 */
96	export function mayTransact(
97	  user: Pick<VerifiableUser, "emailVerifiedAt" | "createdAt">,
98	  mailWorks: boolean,
99	): boolean {
100	  if (isEmailVerified(user)) return true;
101	  if (isGrandfathered(user)) return true;
102	  if (!mailWorks) return true; // fail-open 2: an unpassable gate is not a gate
103	  return false;
104	}
105	
106	/**
107	 * The message a blocked customer sees. Names the address we are waiting on (so a
108	 * typo is visible at the moment it matters) and points at the resend control,
109	 * because "no" without "here is how to say yes" is the dead end we are avoiding.
110	 */
111	export function verificationRequiredMessage(email: string): string {
112	  return `Confirm your email address before buying. We sent a link to ${email} — open it, or send a new one from Settings (Dashboard → Settings → Email address).`;
113	}
114	
115	/**
116	 * THE GATE. Returns a customer-facing message when the action must be refused,
117	 * or `null` to proceed.
118	 *
119	 * Use this in actions that return `{ error?: string }` — most spend paths do —
120	 * so the refusal renders inside the form the customer is already looking at.
121	 * Use `assertEmailVerified` where the action throws instead.
122	 */
123	export async function emailVerificationError(user: VerifiableUser): Promise<string | null> {
124	  if (isEmailVerified(user) || isGrandfathered(user)) return null;
125	  // FAIL-OPEN 0 — the operational master switch, checked before anything else.
126	  //
127	  // This gate turns "our email arrived" into a precondition for taking money, so
128	  // it must not be armed while deliverability cannot be demonstrated. It ships
129	  // OFF: as of 2026-07-26 `dkim._domainkey.nxeon.cloud` is NXDOMAIN, so every
130	  // transactional email this platform sends is unsigned and materially more
131	  // likely to be filtered. A new customer whose link lands in spam would simply
132	  // be unable to buy, and nothing would report it. See the note on
133	  // `email_verification_enforced` in lib/settings.ts.
134	  //
135	  // Checked FIRST, so disabling the gate is unconditional and cheap — an operator
136	  // who turns it off must never have that decision second-guessed downstream.
137	  const { getSettingBool } = await import("./settings");
138	  if (!(await getSettingBool("email_verification_enforced", false))) return null;
139	  const { mailConfigured } = await import("./mailer");
140	  let mailWorks = true;
141	  try {
142	    mailWorks = await mailConfigured();
143	  } catch {
144	    mailWorks = false; // cannot even ask => treat as broken => stand down
145	  }
146	  if (!mailWorks) {
147	    console.warn(
148	      `[email-verification] STANDING DOWN for user ${user.id}: this instance has no mail transport, ` +
149	        `so the verification link can never arrive. Configure SMTP to re-arm the purchase gate.`,
150	    );
151	    return null;
152	  }
153	  return verificationRequiredMessage(user.email);
154	}
155	
156	/**
157	 * Throwing form of the gate, mirroring `assertNotImpersonating` in lib/auth.ts.
158	 * Only for spend paths whose signature has nowhere to put an error string.
159	 */
160	export async function assertEmailVerified(user: VerifiableUser): Promise<void> {
161	  const err = await emailVerificationError(user);
162	  if (err) throw new Error(err);
163	}
164	
165	/* -------------------------------------------------------------------------- */
166	/*                                  Tokens                                    */
167	/* -------------------------------------------------------------------------- */
168	
169	const hashToken = (raw: string) => createHash("sha256").update(raw).digest("hex");
170	
171	/**
172	 * Mint a verification token for `email`.
173	 *
174	 * Only the SHA-256 hash is stored, exactly as `PasswordResetToken` does: a
175	 * database leak must not hand out working links. The address is stored on the
176	 * token too, so a link minted for one address can never verify a different one
177	 * (which is what makes this safe to reuse for a future change-of-address flow).
178	 */
179	export async function issueVerificationToken(userId: string, email: string): Promise<string> {
180	  const raw = randomBytes(32).toString("base64url");
181	  await db.emailVerificationToken.create({
182	    data: {
183	      userId,
184	      email: normalizeEmail(email),
185	      tokenHash: hashToken(raw),
186	      expiresAt: new Date(Date.now() + VERIFICATION_TTL_MS),
187	    },
188	  });
189	  return raw;
190	}
191	
192	export type ConsumeResult = "ok" | "already" | "invalid" | "expired" | "stale";
193	
194	/**
195	 * Redeem a token from a verification link.
196	 *
197	 * `already` (the account is verified) is reported separately from `ok` but is
198	 * NOT an error: people click the same link twice, and mail security scanners
199	 * fetch links before the recipient ever sees them. Both outcomes end with a
200	 * verified account, so both must end on a page that says so.
201	 *
202	 * `stale` means the token was minted for an address the account no longer uses —
203	 * verifying it would assert control of the wrong mailbox.
204	 */
205	export async function consumeVerificationToken(rawToken: string): Promise<ConsumeResult> {
206	  if (!rawToken) return "invalid";
207	  const row = await db.emailVerificationToken.findUnique({ where: { tokenHash: hashToken(rawToken) } });
208	  if (!row) return "invalid";
209	  const user = await db.user.findUnique({ where: { id: row.userId } });
210	  if (!user) return "invalid";
211	  if (normalizeEmail(user.email) !== normalizeEmail(row.email)) return "stale";
212	  if (user.emailVerifiedAt) return "already";
213	  if (row.usedAt) return "invalid";
214	  if (row.expiresAt < new Date()) return "expired";
215	
216	  const now = new Date();
217	  await db.$transaction([
218	    db.user.update({ where: { id: user.id }, data: { emailVerifiedAt: now } }),
219	    db.emailVerificationToken.update({ where: { id: row.id }, data: { usedAt: now } }),
220	    db.auditLog.create({ data: { userId: user.id, action: "user.email_verified", detail: user.email } }),
221	  ]);
222	  return "ok";
223	}
224	
225	/* -------------------------------------------------------------------------- */
226	/*                                  Sending                                   */
227	/* -------------------------------------------------------------------------- */
228	
229	/** Resend throttle: generous enough for a real inbox problem, useless as a cannon. */
230	export const RESEND_LIMIT = { max: 5, windowMs: 60 * 60 * 1000 };
231	
232	export type SendOutcome = "sent" | "already_verified" | "rate_limited" | "failed";
233	
234	/**
235	 * Send (or re-send) the verification link.
236	 *
237	 * The send goes through `sendMail` with `kind: "email_verify"` and the user id,
238	 * which hands the decision to the notification POLICY in lib/prefs.ts rather
239	 * than making it here — that indirection is the whole point of that module. The
240	 * policy classifies this kind CRITICAL, for the same reason it classifies
241	 * `password_reset` CRITICAL: it is the only route to a usable account, so a
242	 * preference checkbox must not be able to make it undeliverable and strand the
243	 * customer behind a gate they were never told how to pass.
244	 */
245	export async function sendVerificationEmail(
246	  user: VerifiableUser,
247	  opts: { throttleKey?: string } = {},
248	): Promise<SendOutcome> {
249	  if (isEmailVerified(user)) return "already_verified";
250	  const rl = checkRateLimit(`emailverify:${opts.throttleKey ?? user.id}`, RESEND_LIMIT);
251	  if (!rl.ok) return "rate_limited";
252	
253	  const token = await issueVerificationToken(user.id, user.email);
254	  const base = process.env.APP_URL ?? "https://nxeon.cloud";
255	  const link = `${base}/api/auth/verify-email?token=${token}`;
256	  const { sendMail, emails } = await import("./mailer");
257	  const tpl = emails.emailVerify(user.name, link);
258	  const ok = await sendMail({
259	    to: user.email,
260	    subject: tpl.subject,
261	    html: tpl.html,
262	    template: tpl.template,
263	    userId: user.id,
264	    kind: "email_verify",
265	  });
266	  return ok ? "sent" : "failed";
267	}

10	/**
11	 * Server actions for the admin settings hub. One entry point, `saveSettings`,
12	 * writes the rows for a single section (tab). Which keys belong to a section —
13	 * and how each is coerced — is described declaratively below so the action never
14	 * trusts the client for the key list.
15	 *
16	 * Coercion rules:
17	 *  - "bool":   checkbox → "true"/"false" (unchecked checkboxes don't POST, so we
18	 *              can't rely on presence alone; every bool key is always written).
19	 *  - "int":    trimmed, validated integer, range-checked; blank restores the default.
20	 *  - "num":    same as "int" but decimals are kept (percent fields).
21	 *  - "enum":   must be one of `values`; anything else is refused.
22	 *  - "secret": only written when non-blank, so a blank field never wipes the
23	 *              stored secret — and stored secrets are never echoed to the client.
24	 *  - "string": trimmed as-is.
25	 *
26	 * WHY THE RANGES AND THE "enum" TYPE EXIST
27	 * ----------------------------------------
28	 * Every numeric field on this page is a free-text box that an operator types into
29	 * once, at speed, usually during an incident — and several of them multiply money
30	 * or gate an irreversible action. The two failures this codebase has already shipped
31	 * were both of exactly this shape: `domain_markup_percent` billed a hardcoded 25%
32	 * while the panel showed 0%, and the auto-suspend kill switch reported "Saved." and
33	 * then let the sweep take customer VMs offline anyway. Both were silent.
34	 *
35	 * So values are validated HERE, at the write, and an out-of-range entry is REFUSED
36	 * with a message naming the allowed range rather than quietly stored or quietly
37	 * clamped. Refusing is the honest option: the row that ends up in the database is
38	 * always exactly the number the operator can see in the field. Where a reader also
39	 * clamps (`lib/registrar.ts` domainMarkupPct, `worker/billing.ts` dunningConfig) the
40	 * bounds below are set to AGREE with it, so the panel can never display one number
41	 * while the platform enforces another — which is the whole defect class this page
42	 * keeps producing.
43	 *
44	 * `enum` matters for the same reason: a `<select>` constrains a browser, not a
45	 * request. A hand-crafted POST could otherwise store `currency: "'; DROP"` or a
46	 * `default_term` no charge path understands.
47	 */
48	
49	type FieldType = "string" | "bool" | "int" | "num" | "secret" | "enum";
50	type Field = {
51	  key: string;
52	  type: FieldType;
53	  /** Inclusive bounds for "int"/"num". Out of range is refused, not clamped. */
54	  min?: number;
55	  max?: number;
56	  /** Permitted values for "enum". */
57	  values?: readonly string[];
58	};
59	
60	const CURRENCIES = ["USD", "EUR", "GBP", "CAD", "AUD"] as const;
61	
62	/**
63	 * Permitted `default_term` values: the MONTH COUNTS the platform actually sells, derived
64	 * from `VPS_TERMS` so this list cannot drift from the deploy wizard's own buttons.
65	 *
66	 * This was `["monthly", "quarterly", "annual"]` — the vocabulary the comment at the top of
67	 * this file warned about ("a `default_term` no charge path understands"). It was worse than
68	 * unreadable: "quarterly" names a term that does not exist anywhere in the catalogue, and
69	 * the enum could not express the 24- and 36-month terms that do. Storing months, validated
70	 * against the single source of truth, is what made wiring the setting possible at all.
71	 *
72	 * A legacy "monthly"/"annual" row is no longer accepted on write and is ignored on read —
73	 * `defaultTermMonths()` falls back to the first term rather than pre-selecting a
74	 * commitment `vpsTerm()` would silently reprice.
75	 */
76	const TERMS = VPS_TERMS.map((t) => String(t.months)) as readonly string[];

84	 * − 1) + 1 + 4 + 1 = 11, with DUNNING_RETRY_ATTEMPTS = 3 in `lib/mailer.ts`. Those
85	 * constants are module-private over there, so this cannot be imported; it is
86	 * duplicated deliberately and named so it is greppable if the retry schedule changes.

88	 * It is enforced here so the panel cannot DISPLAY a termination day earlier than the
89	 * one the worker will actually honour. Drift is safe in one direction only: the
90	 * worker's own clamp merely raises `terminateDays`, so a stale floor here costs a

172	    { key: "signup_free_credit_cents", type: "int", min: 0, max: 100_000 },
173	    // Node capacity warning thresholds (whole percents). Bounds 1..100: 0 would
174	    // trip every node on the first sweep; nodeThresholds() additionally clamps

177	    { key: "node_critical_pct", type: "int", min: 1, max: 100 },
178	    { key: "maintenance_mode", type: "bool" },
179	    { key: "maintenance_message", type: "string" },

221	/** Sections that are billing-adjacent are gated on the "billing" area; the rest
222	 *  on "platform". BILLING-role staff may thus edit money-facing knobs. */
223	const BILLING_SECTIONS = new Set(["billing", "domains", "dedicated-ip"]);
224	
225	type Result = { ok?: boolean; error?: string };
226	
227	/**
228	 * Persist one section of settings. Bind the section server-side in the panel
229	 * (`saveSettings.bind(null, "general")`) so it's never client-supplied; React's
230	 * useActionState then supplies (prevState, formData).
231	 */
232	export async function saveSettings(
233	  section: string,
234	  _prev: Result | undefined,
235	  formData: FormData,
236	): Promise<Result> {
237	  const fields = SECTION_FIELDS[section];
238	  if (!fields) return { error: "Unknown settings section." };
239	
240	  const area = BILLING_SECTIONS.has(section) ? "billing" : "platform";
241	  const user = await requireArea(area);
242	
243	  const changes: { key: string; value: string }[] = [];
244	
245	  for (const f of fields) {
246	    const raw = formData.get(f.key);
247	
248	    if (f.type === "bool") {
249	      changes.push({ key: f.key, value: raw ? "true" : "false" });
250	      continue;
251	    }
252	
253	    if (f.type === "secret") {
254	      const v = (raw ?? "").toString();
255	      if (v.trim() === "") continue; // never clear/overwrite a stored secret with blank
256	      // Encrypt at rest. `smtp_pass` was the last secret in the DB stored as
257	      // plaintext while mailbox passwords and the Cloudflare token both use the
258	      // AES-256-GCM box. Read-back in lib/mailer.ts decrypts, tolerating a legacy
259	      // plaintext row until it is next saved. Never render — SecretField shows
260	      // only `isSet` — so this closes an at-rest exposure, not a live leak.
261	      changes.push({ key: f.key, value: encryptSecret(v) });
262	      continue;
263	    }
264	
265	    if (f.type === "enum") {
266	      const s = (raw ?? "").toString().trim();
267	      if (s === "") {
268	        changes.push({ key: f.key, value: SETTINGS_DEFAULTS[f.key as keyof typeof SETTINGS_DEFAULTS] ?? "" });
269	        continue;
270	      }
271	      // A <select> constrains the browser, not the request.
272	      if (!f.values?.includes(s)) {
273	        return { error: `“${f.key}” must be one of: ${f.values?.join(", ")}.` };
274	      }
275	      changes.push({ key: f.key, value: s });
276	      continue;
277	    }
278	
279	    if (f.type === "int" || f.type === "num") {
280	      const s = (raw ?? "").toString().trim();
281	      if (s === "") {
282	        changes.push({ key: f.key, value: SETTINGS_DEFAULTS[f.key as keyof typeof SETTINGS_DEFAULTS] ?? "0" });
283	        continue;
284	      }
285	      const n = Number(s);
286	      if (!Number.isFinite(n)) return { error: `“${f.key}” must be a number.` };
287	      // Refuse rather than clamp, so the stored row always equals what the operator
288	      // can read back off the field. Silent clamping is how a panel ends up showing
289	      // one number while the platform enforces another.
290	      if (f.min !== undefined && n < f.min) {
291	        return { error: `“${f.key}” must be at least ${f.min} (you entered ${s}).` };
292	      }
293	      if (f.max !== undefined && n > f.max) {
294	        return { error: `“${f.key}” must be ${f.max} or less (you entered ${s}).` };
295	      }
296	      changes.push({ key: f.key, value: f.type === "int" ? String(Math.round(n)) : String(n) });
297	      continue;
298	    }
299	
300	    changes.push({ key: f.key, value: (raw ?? "").toString().trim() });
301	  }
302	
303	  // Cross-field: the dunning schedule must run in the order the panel's own hints
304	  // promise — grace (dunning starts) ≤ warn (final-warning email) < terminate (VM
305	  // destroyed). Field-level bounds cannot catch an inverted schedule, and an
306	  // inverted one deletes a customer's server before, or without, warning them.
307	  // worker/billing.ts also clamps on read; this check exists so the operator is
308	  // TOLD, instead of having their numbers silently rewritten behind the panel.
309	  if (section === "billing") {
310	    const day = (k: string) => Number(changes.find((c) => c.key === k)?.value);
311	    const grace = day("dunning_grace_days");
312	    const warn = day("dunning_warn_days");
313	    const terminate = day("dunning_terminate_days");
314	    if (warn < grace) {
315	      return { error: `Dunning warn (${warn}d) cannot come before dunning grace (${grace}d).` };
316	    }
317	    if (terminate <= warn) {
318	      return { error: `Dunning terminate (${terminate}d) must come after the final warning (${warn}d).` };
319	    }
320	  }
321	
322	  if (changes.length === 0) return { ok: true };
323	
324	  await db.$transaction(
325	    changes.map((c) =>
326	      db.setting.upsert({ where: { key: c.key }, update: { value: c.value }, create: { key: c.key, value: c.value } }),
327	    ),
328	  );
329	
330	  await db.auditLog.create({
331	    data: {
332	      userId: user.id,
333	      action: "settings.save",
334	      detail: `${section}: ${changes.map((c) => c.key).join(", ")}`,
335	    },
336	  });
337	
338	  revalidatePath("/admin/settings");
339	  return { ok: true };
340	}

I've completed the audit: core auth files read directly, all customer + admin server-action files swept (45 files across three parallel passes plus my own reads), and every dynamic/public API route checked. Here is the verdict.

---

# Nxeon Auth / Session / RBAC / IDOR Audit — Findings

## Overall verdict: STRONG. No CRITICAL/HIGH/MEDIUM issues found.

This is an unusually well-hardened codebase. It carries visible scar tissue from prior audits (QA-PRELAUNCH P0-2, AUDIT-24H, etc.), and the classic vulnerability classes you asked me to hunt are not just absent — they're absent *with documented reasoning* at each fix site. I actively tried to find the anti-patterns and could not produce a single concrete IDOR or privilege-escalation exploit. Below is what I verified, then the only (low/informational) observations worth recording.

## 1. Account takeover — CLEAN
- **Password reset** (`lib/actions-account.ts:128-213`): token is `randomBytes(32)` base64url (256-bit), stored only as SHA-256 hash, single-use (`usedAt`), 1h expiry, bound to `userId`. `resetPassword` bumps `sessionVersion` (evicts old sessions). No user enumeration: constant `{sent:true}` response, rate-limited per email+IP, and the mail send is **deliberately un-awaited** to kill the timing oracle (documented at :158-168).
- **Login/register** (`lib/actions.ts:156-333`): login spends a dummy bcrypt compare on missing accounts (`DUMMY_PASSWORD_HASH`, :129) to close the enumeration timing gap; rate-limit keyed on `clientIp()` (nginx-appended, not client-forgeable XFF).
- **2FA/TOTP** (`lib/actions-2fa.ts`, `lib/totp-verify.ts`): `verifyTotpForUser` is deliberately kept out of any `"use server"` file (was previously an unauthenticated brute-force oracle — the P0-2 fix). TOTP codes are single-use via `claimOnce` (RFC 6238 §5.2), backup codes consumed with a compare-and-swap `updateMany`.
- **Session/cookies** (`lib/auth.ts`): JWT via `jose` HS256 (no `alg:none` / impersonation-token confusion — `assertSessionToken` blocks promotion of the 2h imp grant into a session); cookie is `httpOnly`, `sameSite:lax`, `secure` in production. `sessionVersion` embedded for revocation. Impersonation re-checks suspended/ADMIN against the *current* row every request.

## 2. Privilege escalation / mass-assignment — CLEAN
- Admin surface gated three ways: `app/admin/layout.tsx` (host allowlist → `realUser` → `isStaff` → refuses impersonation → IP allowlist → staff-2FA), **and** every admin server action self-gates with `requireAdmin()`/`requireStaff()`/`requireArea()` at its first statement. All ~40 coldemail, all board, staff, nodes, admin-billing, agency, ads, abuse, improvements actions verified gated.
- **No mass-assignment anywhere.** `updateProfile` writes only `name`; `saveSettings` uses a declarative `SECTION_FIELDS` allowlist with per-field coercion/enums (a hand-crafted POST can't set an unlisted key); `setUserRole` validates against a zod enum and blocks self-demotion; `updateNotificationPrefs` pins `security:true` and takes no client user id. No action spreads untrusted input into a Prisma `create`/`update` — every `data:` object is explicitly field-listed, and `role`/`userId`/`balanceCents`/`status` are never set from request input.

## 3. IDOR (priority) — CLEAN
Every dynamic API route and every id-taking server action scopes the resource to the caller before read/mutate:
- **API routes** — `invoices/[id]` + `/pdf`, `domains/[id]/dns-export`, `servers/[id]/disk`, `servers/[id]/backups/download` (double guard: ownership + volid∈`listBackups(vmid)`), `files/[serverId]`, `console/[serverId]`, `terminal/token`, `metrics?serverId=`, `claude/[id]`, `hosting/files`, `mail/attachment`, `chat/[id]` (scoped by `visitorId`), `chat/attachment/[id]`, `account/export`, `admin/export` (per-`type` `canAccess`) — all verify `userId === session.user.id` (or admin) first. `mail/signature-image/[id]` and `coldemail/track/*` are intentionally public (unguessable cuid / email pixels), returning only image bytes with `default-src 'none'` CSP.
- **Server actions** — consistent `ownedServer`/`ownedDatabase`/`ownedApp`/`ownedCron`/`ownedCertificate`/`ownedDomain`/`ownedVolume`/`ownedSchedule`/`resolveMailbox`/`loadOwned` helpers, each verified to check ownership *before* returning the row; delete-by-id paths use `deleteMany({where:{id, userId}})` or join back through an owned parent, so a bare client id is never the sole predicate.

---

## Low / informational observations (no action strictly required)

- **LOW — No `middleware.ts`; admin authz is fully decentralized.** Protection depends on the admin layout wrapping child pages *and* every admin action/route self-gating. Today all of them do (verified). The residual risk is purely future-facing: one new admin action that forgets `requireAdmin()` is a hole, and unlike `/api/v1` (which has a test tripwire asserting scope checks), there is no equivalent automated guard for admin server actions/routes. Consider an analogous test asserting every `app/api/admin/**` and admin action gates.
- **LOW (defense-in-depth) — Calendar** (`lib/actions-calendar.ts`): the by-href update/delete paths (`updateEvent`, `deleteEvent`, `setTaskCompleted`, `deleteTask`) rely on SOGo's per-principal CalDAV ACL for object-level ownership rather than an explicit `assertOwnedCalendar` (which the create paths *do* call). Not a Prisma IDOR — the CalDAV credential is user-scoped — but an explicit check before those writes would harden against a CalDAV ACL misconfiguration.
- **INFO — Admin IP allowlist and host gate both fail-open** by design (documented): a malformed `allowed_admin_ips` or an undeterminable requester IP allows access rather than locking admins out. Acceptable operationally, but they are convenience layers, not a security boundary — the real gate is `isStaff`/`requireArea`.
- **INFO — `resetPassword` token submission isn't rate-limited**, but the token is 256-bit random, so brute force is infeasible; not exploitable.

Net: the auth posture here is well above typical for a pre-launch platform. I'd class it production-ready on the auth/session/RBAC/IDOR axis, with the two LOW items as hardening backlog rather than blockers.
